newsitem.title: GERMANY: Director Spike Lee laments barriers to black films.
newsitem.headline: Director Spike Lee laments barriers to black films.

text.p: Director Spike Lee said on Tuesday he was annoyed his films that focus on African-American issues were often withheld from foreign markets by distributors who failed to see the universal appeal of the stories.

Speaking at the 47th annual Berlin Film Festival where his film "Get On The Bus" made its international premiere, Lee said Hollywood executives were wrong to assume foreign audiences were not interested in African-American subjects.

"There is a mentality that African-American films don't play well outside the United States," Lee said at a news conference after his film received warm applause from a crowd of some 1,000 critics and journalists from around the world.

"They (studio executives) say that and it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. They believe that is the way it is and so they make sure those films don't make it outside the U.S. If it doesn't have Eddie Murphy, they think it won't play abroad."

Many of Lee's earlier films such as "Do The Right Thing" and "She's Gotta Have It" received critical acclaim in Europe and have been fixtures at the Cannes, Berlin and Venice festivals. But few have had strong box office runs in foreign territories.

"I think African-American films could do well in Europe," Lee said. "I wouldn't be here if I didn't believe that. That is why we are here in Berlin. We are not interested in awards as much as using this festival as a launching pad for the release of the film in Europe."

Saying he was perplexed about the perceived barriers to the market interest in African-American subject matter, Lee said he admired the universal themes in films from directors such as Federico Fellini Italy and Rainer Werner Fassbinder of Germany.

"I am often asked when am I going to do a 'mainstream' film," Lee said. "That really makes me wonder. I feel the films I've done are universal. Just because the actors are black shouldn't be a hindrance to anyone seeing and enjoying the film.
"Nobody ever asked Fassbinder that question and no one ever asked Fellini to do a film that has nothing to do with Italians," Lee added.

"I don't understand a word of Italian but I love his films. I was not born in Italy. I am making films about African-Americans and people say 'Oh there goes Spike again with that black stuff again'. I am going to go to my grave and not understand it."
Lee's film "Get On The Bus" is a fictional story about a diverse group of African-Americans journeying from Los Angeles to Washington for the 1995 "Million-Man-March" demonstration.

Among those boarding the bus as strangers for the three-day journey are an estranged father trying to bond with his teenage son, an aspiring actor filled with hatred, a police officer fed up with urban slaughter, and a businessman who supports the conservative Republican party.
